         2                  "WHEREAS, With the terrible attack

         3       of our nation on September 11, 2001, still so

         4       painfully fresh in our hearts and minds, it is

         5       more important than ever that we reflect on

         6       the strength and heritage of our great

         7       country.  We owe a debt of gratitude and

         8       remembrance to our immigrant forebears and,

         9       while the Triangle toll was a grievous wound

        10       for our Jewish and Italian grandparents and

        11       ancestors, all should join together to record,

        12       remember and memorialize the sacrifices and

        13       courage of all the immigrants who built this

        14       nation so that their children and descendants

        15       would reap the rewards of their achievements

        16       and enjoy the benefits of life and liberty in

        17       America, the greatest country in the world;

        19                  "WHEREAS, At the turn of the

        20       century, urban working conditions in the

        21       United States were appalling.  Noplace else

        22       were these conditions more deplorable than in

        23       New York's garment industry.  Here, young

        24       women, mostly recent immigrants, toiled from

         1       dawn to dusk.  In the winter of 1909, a strike

         2       was organized; the union believed that if it

         3       could get 3,000 workers to go out on strike,

         4       the strike would be successful.  Amazingly,

         5       20,000 women, including workers from the

         6       Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, joined the

         7       strike, but despite their courageous efforts,

         8       the conditions did not improve; and

         9                  "WHEREAS, The shirtwaist was the

        10       uniform of the new woman.  The first women to

        11       go out to work as 'typewriters' wore it; so

        12       did the 'Gibson Girls' that Charles Dana

        13       Gibson drew playing golf or croquet.  It was

        14       the first civilian garment simple and loosely

        15       fitted enough to be made in factories by the

        16       dozens, instead of custom-made one at a time

        17       by dressmakers or tailors; and

        18                  "WHEREAS, By the early 1890s,

        19       shirtwaists were being made in modern

        20       factories, at long rows of sewing machines

        21       powered by electricity.  Max Blanck and Isaac

        22       Harris, owners of the million-dollar Triangle

        23       Shirtwaist Company, with operations in

        24       New York and Philadelphia, were the



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                (518) 371-8910
                                                         1402



         1       'shirtwaist kings.'  Their biggest factory

         2       occupied the top three floors of a new,

         3       fireproof building a block from Washington

         4       Square in New York and employed approximately

         5       600 people; and

         6                  "WHEREAS, The employees were

         7       putting on their hats and coats at quitting

         8       time on Saturday, March 25, 1911, when someone

         9       noticed smoke curling from the long rag bin

        10       under the under the cutting tables along the

        11       windows on the eighth floor.  The month's

        12       accumulation of linen and muslin scraps caught

        13       fire, then the fabric that was laid out on the

        14       tables, then the paper patterns strung open on

        15       the wire above them, then the big wicker

        16       baskets full of bundled work that stood by

        17       each sewing machine; and

        18                  "WHEREAS, There were no sprinklers;

        19       only three weeks before, an association of

        20       property owners had met to oppose the fire

        21       department's campaign to require them; and

        22                  "WHEREAS, In the Triangle fire, all

        23       but one of the terrified seamstresses and

        24       cutters on the eighth floor escaped, whether

                                                         1403



         1       by one of the two small elevators or down one

         2       of the building's two narrow stairways, each

         3       wide enough for only one person to descend at

         4       a time.  Somebody telephoned a warning to the

         5       executives on the 10th floor, where the fire

         6       quickly spread, and many from the offices and

         7       the pressing and shipping rooms on the

         8       10th floor, including the shirtwaist factory

         9       owners themselves, caught an elevator or

        10       escaped over the roof; and

        11                  "WHEREAS, Tragically, nobody told

        12       the ninth floor.  By the time they knew, they

        13       were caught between fires above and below

        14       them.  Some ran for the elevators, others for

        15       the doors to the stairs.  One set of doors was

        16       locked to keep girls from leaving early.  The

        17       doors to the other stairway opened inward, and

        18       almost immediately the terrified crush made it

        19       impossible to open them.  Soon the stairs were

        20       cut off by the fire; and

        21                  "WHEREAS, The elevator operators

        22       did their best, each making seven or eight

        23       trips through smoke and flames.  But as the

        24       fire grew, it forced one after another of the



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                (518) 371-8910
                                                         1404



         1       desperate waiting crowds of girls and young

         2       women to leap into the open shaft, until

         3       finally the elevators could not rise because

         4       they were jammed by bodies; and

         5                  "WHEREAS, The rest of the

         6       ninth-floor workers were forced to the

         7       windows.  They stood on the ledges as long as

         8       they could, waiting for the fire ladders, but

         9       the city's longest ladder reached only to the

        10       sixth floor.  And as the fire reached out the

        11       windows after them, they began to jump, many

        12       holding hands, to their deaths on the

        13       sidewalks and fences below; and

        14                  "WHEREAS, The date March 25th holds

        15       a special significance for all working people

        16       because of this tragic Triangle Shirtwaist

        17       Factory Fire in New York City that took the

        18       lives of 146 garment workers, a tragedy that

        19       occurred on March 25, 1911; and

        20                  "WHEREAS, Among those lost were

        21       many sisters, mothers, daughters and family

        22       groups, including Mrs. Caterina Maltese and

        23       her daughters, Lucia and Rosaria; and

        24                  "WHEREAS, This tragedy became the



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                (518) 371-8910
                                                         1405



         1       most vivid signal of the need for workplace

         2       safety and spawned the labor movement.  The

         3       Factory Investigating Commission was formed

         4       following the fire to study and make

         5       recommendations on working conditions.  This

         6       marked the beginning of auspicious political

         7       careers for both the chairman, Robert T.

         8       Wagner, Sr., who went on to become a U.S.

         9       Senator, and its vice chairman, Alfred E.

        10       Smith, who became New York State Governor.  In

        11       addition, among the investigating inspectors

        12       were Frances Perkins and Rose Schneiderman,

        13       women who were pivotal in the history of

        14       American labor.  The findings of the

        15       commission became the basis for far-reaching

        16       safety laws across the nation and forged the

        17       New York State Department of Labor.  The

        18       Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire started a

        19       movement to fight sweatshops which continues

        20       to this day; and

        22       thanks largely to the efforts of architect

         1       in supporting this resolution.  Ninety-eight

         2       years ago next Wednesday, March the 25th, one

         3       of the most horrifying industrial disasters in

         4       the history of New York State claimed the

         5       lives of 146 workers in the Triangle

         6       Shirtwaist Factory Fire in Greenwich Village.

         7                  At 4:30 in the afternoon, when the

         8       fire broke out on the eighth floor of the

         9       10-story building and quickly spread to the

        10       ninth and 10th floors, frantic young immigrant

        11       workers either perished in the flames,

        12       suffocated, or jumped out of the factory

        13       windows to their deaths.

        14                  Of the 500 workers in the factory

        15       that day, almost 150 were lost.  Even the fire

        16       trucks that responded to the scene were of

        17       little help.  Their ladders and hoses only

        18       reached to the sixth floor.

        19                  And all this happened in a building

        20       that had been locked from the outside to keep

        21       the sweatshop humming along and keep the

        22       workers from leaving the factory during their

        23       shifts.

        24                  These workers began their long



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                (518) 371-8910
                                                         1411



         1       factory shifts that day underpaid, exploited,

         2       unprotected from employer abuse, and they

         3       ended their shifts in agony and in tragedy.

         4                  While it may be close to impossible

         5       to imagine the horror of that day, it is

         6       vitally important that we never forget the

         7       victims of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory

         8       Fire.  And that is what we are doing here

         9       today in the New York State Senate.

        10                  While government action came too

        11       late to help the 146 who perished, new laws

        12       were passed in New York State to provide

        13       needed protections for workers and new safety

        14       standards in the factories.  The deaths of the

        15       Triangle Shirtwaist Factory workers, while

        16       horrific, surely helped to save the lives of

        17       many workers of their generation and workers

        18       of the future.

        19                  The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory

        20       tragedy also helped spur the growth of the

        21       International Ladies' Garment Workers Union,

        22       helping to provide a strong voice for those

        23       whose pleas for safety, fair wages and

        24       reasonable work hours and other basic worker
